newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left wants Europe to focus on social issues.
newsitem.headline: French left wants Europe to focus on social issues.

text.p: French Socialist and Communist leaders said on Tuesday they were against a free-market Europe and called for talks with France's partners to refocus European integration on social issues.
The leaders of the two opposition parties met to discuss a joint electoral declaration ahead of a parliamentary election on May 25/June 1.

"We say no to a liberal (free-market) Europe, to the Europe where money is king, and to submission to financial markets. We think we must give back a meaning to Europe by going beyond the Maastricht treaty," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist leader Robert Hue said in a joint statement released after the talks.
"We think France must urge its European partners to embark on talks with the aim of...redirecting European integration towards a social Europe for progress, peace and security," they said.
The statement did not try to reconcile differences between the parties on the introduction of a single European currency.
It simply said: "The respective positions of the Socialist Party and the Communist Party on Europe are well known."

While the Socialists are in favour of the euro, albeit with conditions, the Communists have called for a fresh referendum, branding monetary union an "ultra-liberal political project." Jospin reiterated his commitment to the single currency on Tuesday, but repeated the Socialists would not enter European economic and monetary union without certain conditions being met.

"We are in favour of monetary union, but we don't want a dogmatic reading of the Maastricht treaty," Jospin said at a news conference. "If these conditions are met, it's 'yes'. If these conditions are not met, it's 'no'."

The Socialists have laid down four conditions for taking part in single currency: entry for any European Union member who wants to join, the creation of an "economic government", the setting up of an EU pact of solidarity and growth to create jobs, and that the euro should not be overvalued against the dollar.
Jospin also said he believed the Communists' approach towards European issues was evolving. He gave no details.
